name: Sorrel (hibiscus) drink
what_people_do: Steep dried sorrel calyces (Hibiscus sabdariffa) with ginger and cloves, sweeten and chill; a Christmas staple in Jamaica and drunk through the year; known as zobo or sobolo in West Africa.
why_they_say_it_works: It is said to be cooling, good for the heart and "pressure", and rich in vitamin C.

documented_by.source: 'Sorrel, both delicious and nutritious', Jamaica Gleaner, 22 Dec 2014 (opened 12 Nov 2026)
documented_by.quote_or_summary: Jamaica Gleaner health column: popular year-round, made by steeping the whole calyx; traditional uses listed as diuretic, tonic, cough remedy; says it is said to lower blood pressure, but cites no study.

evidence.population: Umbrella review and meta-analysis of 26 RCTs, 1,797 adults (Iran, Mexico, Egypt, Nigeria and others, not diaspora-specific)
evidence.finding: Dose-dependent fall in systolic and diastolic pressure vs placebo; no significant difference vs antihypertensive drugs; moderate credibility for a fall of more than 10 mmHg.

source.name: Norouzzadeh M et al 2025, Complement Ther Med, PMID 39870328

harm_note: Can add to blood pressure drugs; sweetened versions add sugar; a minor, clinically insignificant rise in AST was noted in one analysis. The Gleaner claims about cancer are uncited.
gaps: Home sorrel drinks are heavily sweetened; trial doses are unsweetened tea or extract.
